response: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) continues the principle found in the Indian Evidence Act (IEA) regarding confessions made to police officers. Under the BSA, specifically Section 23, no confession made to a police officer shall be proved against a person accused of any offence, and no confession made while in police custody (unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate) can be proved against the accused. This is similar to the repealed Section 25 and Section 26 of the IEA, which also barred confessions to police officers and confessions made in police custody from being proved against the accused. The wording and the effect of the provisions remain consistent, thus the BSA upholds the legal safeguards against using police confessions, just as the IEA did.

[BNS Section 111(2):] Whoever commits organised crime shall,—(i) if such offence has resulted in the death of any person, be punishable with death or imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine of not less than ten lakh rupees; (ii) in any other case, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine of not less than five lakh rupees.

response:
Under the Indian Evidence Act (IEA), Section 45 stated that when the Court has to form an opinion on a point of foreign law, science, art, or as to the identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in those areas are relevant facts, and these persons are called experts. The same section included an illustration regarding the relevance of expert opinions in cases like determining cause of death by poison [IEA | repealed | evidentiary | Section 45].

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) has retained the same rule in Section 39. It states, in nearly identical terms, that when the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, science, art, any other field, or identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions of persons specially skilled in those fields are relevant facts and such persons are called experts, with the same type of illustration provided [BSA | active | evidentiary | Section 39].

Thus, the BSA reflects the same principles regarding expert opinions as were found in the IEA, and there is no substantive change in this rule between the two statutes.

Such persons are called experts. [BSA Section 39:] (1) When the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science or art, or any other field, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or any other field, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions are relevant facts and such persons are called experts. (2) When in a proceeding, the court has to form an opinion on any matter relating to any information transmitted or stored in any computer resource or any other electronic or digital form, the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence referred to in section 79A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000), is a relevant fact. Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section, an Examiner of Electronic Evidence shall be an expert. [Key differences: BSA adds 'any other field' broadening expert opinion beyond law/science/art; explicitly adds Examiners of Electronic Evidence as recognised experts for digital/computer evidence.]

response:
Under the CrPC, a judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction had to be pronounced in open court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time with due notice to the parties or their pleaders. The pronouncement could be done by delivering, reading out, or explaining the judgment (or its operative part) in a language understood by the accused or their pleader. If delivered as a written judgment, the presiding officer was required to cause it to be written in shorthand, sign each page, and note the date of delivery in open court [CrPC | repealed | procedural | Section 353].

Under the BNSS, for judgments in appeal by a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate, the rules for pronouncing judgments as per the relevant Chapter (which governs original trial judgments) still apply as far as practicable. However, the BNSS provides that unless the appellate court specifically directs otherwise, the accused does not need to be brought up or attend the pronouncement of the appellate judgment [BNSS | active | procedural | Section 428].

Thus, the core requirements for pronouncement in original trials remain aligned, but BNSS clarifies that the personal attendance of the accused is not generally required at the pronouncement of appellate judgments unless directed by the court.
reference: [CrPC Section 353(1):] The judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time of which notice shall be given to the parties or their advocates. [CrPC had no fixed time limit for pronouncement after the conclusion of trial.] [BNSS Section 392(1):] The judgment in every trial in any Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time not later than forty-five days of which notice shall be given to the parties or their advocates—(a) by delivering the whole of the judgment; or (b) by reading out the whole of the judgment; or (c) by reading out the operative part of the judgment and explaining the substance of the judgment in a language which is understood by the accused or his advocate. [Key difference: BNSS introduces a mandatory 45-day outer limit for pronouncing judgment after conclusion of trial; CrPC had no such time limit.]

reference: [CrPC Section 167:] CrPC contained no express provision permitting production of the accused via video conferencing or audio-video means. The accused was required to be physically produced before the Magistrate for each remand (whether police custody or judicial custody). Some High Courts allowed video conferencing under inherent jurisdiction, but no explicit statutory authorization existed in CrPC. [BNSS Section 187(4):] No Magistrate shall authorise detention of the accused in custody of the police under this section unless the accused is produced before him in person for the first time and subsequently every time till the accused remains in the custody of the police, but the Magistrate may extend further detention in judicial custody on production of the accused either in person or through the audio-video electronic means. [Key change: BNSS expressly permits audio-video electronic production for judicial custody remand extensions. However, for the first appearance and all police custody remands, physical production before the Magistrate remains mandatory.]
